{{Short description|Mathematical polynomial factorization}}
{{about|a polynomial identity attributed to Sophie Germain|the pseudonymous identity used by Germain|Antoine-Auguste Le Blanc}}
{{Use mdy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=June 2023}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=June 2023}}
In mathematics, '''Sophie Germain's identity''' is a [[polynomial factorization]] named after [[Sophie Germain]] stating that
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
x^4 + 4y^4 &= \bigl((x + y)^2 + y^2\bigr)\cdot\bigl((x - y)^2 + y^2\bigr)\\
           &= (x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2)\cdot(x^2 - 2xy + 2y^2).
\end{align}</math>
Beyond its use in [[elementary algebra]], it can also be used in [[number theory]] to [[Integer factorization|factorize integers]] of the special form <math>x^4+4y^4</math>, and it frequently forms the basis of problems in [[mathematics competition]]s.{{r|mgc|crux|engel}}

==History==
Although the identity has been attributed to Sophie Germain, it does not appear in her works. Instead, in her works one can find the related identity{{r|lss|totd}}
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
x^4+y^4 &= (x^2-y^2)^2+2(xy)^2\\
        &= (x^2+y^2)^2-2(xy)^2.\\
\end{align}</math>
Modifying this equation by multiplying <math>y</math> by <math>\sqrt2</math> gives
<math display=block>
x^4+4y^4 = (x^2+2y^2)^2-4(xy)^2,
</math>
a [[difference of two squares]], from which Germain's identity follows.{{r|totd}} The inaccurate attribution of this identity to Germain was made by [[Leonard Eugene Dickson]] in his ''[[History of the Theory of Numbers]]'', which also stated (equally inaccurately) that it could be found in a letter from [[Leonhard Euler]] to [[Christian Goldbach]].{{r|totd|dickson}}

The identity can be proven simply by multiplying the two terms of the factorization together, and verifying that their product equals the right hand side of the equality.{{r|cut}} A [[proof without words]] is also possible based on multiple applications of the [[Pythagorean theorem]].{{r|mgc}} 

==Applications to integer factorization==
One consequence of Germain's identity is that the numbers of the form
<math display=block>n^4+4^n</math>
cannot be [[Prime number|prime]] for <math>n>1</math>. (For <math>n=1</math>, the result is the prime number 5.) They are obviously not prime if <math>n</math> is even, and if <math>n</math> is odd they have a factorization given by the identity with <math>x=n</math> and <math>y=2^{(n-1)/2}</math>.{{r|engel|cut}} These numbers (starting with <math>n=0</math>) form the [[integer sequence]]
{{bi|left=1.6|1, 5, 32, 145, 512, 1649, 5392, 18785, 69632, ... {{OEIS|A001589}}.}}
Many of the appearances of Sophie Germain's identity in mathematics competitions come from this corollary of it.{{r|crux|engel}}

Another special case of the identity with <math>x=1</math> and <math>y=2^k</math>
can be used to produce the factorization
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
\Phi_4(2^{2k+1})&=2^{4k+2}+1\\
&=(2^{2k+1}-2^{k+1}+1)\cdot (2^{2k+1}+2^{k+1}+1),\\
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\Phi_4(x)=x^2+1</math> is the fourth [[cyclotomic polynomial]]. As with the cyclotomic polynomials more generally, <math>\Phi_4</math> is an [[irreducible polynomial]], so this factorization of infinitely many of its values cannot be extended to a factorization of <math>\Phi_4</math> as a polynomial, making this an example of an [[aurifeuillean factorization]].{{r|gp}}

==Generalization==
Germain's identity has been generalized to the [[functional equation]]
<math display=block>
f(x)^2+4f(y)^2 = \bigl( f(x+y)+f(y) \bigr)\bigl(f(x-y)+f(y)\bigr),
</math>
which by Sophie Germain's identity is satisfied by the [[square function]].{{r|lss}}
